63:1.heading: Ayah 1

blocks.text: When the hypocrites come to you, they say, “We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah” And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are truly liars.

The surah opens with the hypocrites approaching the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and immediately insisting that they belong among the believers. Their emphatic testimony reveals hearts troubled by doubt, always needing to prove that they fit into their surroundings and to please opposing sides. When the believers are strong, they make a great display of faith; when the believers are weakened, their words and positions change.

Their testimony about the Messenger is itself true, so Allah first affirms his messengership before declaring the hypocrites liars. Their lie concerns the mismatch between their tongues and their hearts, not the reality of his mission. This reveals how believers and hypocrites differ when circumstances change: believers draw steadfastness and dignity from the faith within them; circumstances do not create their beliefs. Hypocrites derive their position from the surrounding balance of power, so they remain hesitant and changeable as that balance shifts.

63:2.heading: Ayah 2

blocks.text: They have taken their oaths as a shield in order to hinder people from the way of Allah. Evil indeed is what they do!

Their oaths have ceased to be acts of worship and reverence for Allah; they have become a shield that protects them and preserves their standing within the believing community. They exploit believers’ reverence for Allah’s name and reluctance to accuse someone who swears by Him. That protection then enables obstruction of His path. This obstruction has several interpretations that should not be reduced to one: their professed faith shields them from the application of Allah’s judgment to them; people who see them counted among believers may be repelled by their conduct, mistakenly taking it to represent the religion; and they undermine striving in Allah’s cause through discouragement, withdrawal and weakening the ranks.

In all these cases, the shield that protects its bearer also becomes a means of harming others. The verse therefore ends with severe condemnation: among the worst deeds is becoming a cause of obstructing the practice of Allah’s religion or driving people away from it.

63:3.heading: Ayah 3

blocks.text: That is because they believed, then disbelieved; therefore their hearts have been sealed, so they do not understand.

Their initial belief admits two interpretations: some may truly have entered faith and then turned back before it became firmly rooted in their hearts; or they may have professed faith from the outset without its reality ever entering their hearts. The warning extends beyond a person wholly given over to hypocrisy. A single hypocritical trait can begin to grow and accumulate if it is not resisted. The Hadith about four traits of hypocrisy includes this warning: “whoever has one trait of them has one of the traits of hypocrisy until he gives it up” A believer must therefore not treat hypocrisy as something entirely separate that could never affect them, but must examine themselves for lying, betrayal of trust, treachery and wrongdoing in disputes.

Repeatedly treating faith lightly, giving it precedence or setting it aside according to personal advantage, leads to the heart being sealed. The problem then is not merely a lack of information: it is the loss of the understanding through which the heart recognizes the truths of faith and benefits from them.

63:4.heading: Ayah 4

blocks.text: When you see them, their outward appearance pleases you, and when they speak, you listen to what they say. But they are like planks of wood leaned [against the wall][1]. They deem every cry to be against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them. May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?

The description joins outward brilliance to inward emptiness. The hypocrite invests in an impressive appearance and polished speech, seeming strong, generous and noble before being put to the test, while neglecting the purification of the inner self and the treatment of the heart’s diseases. The image of propped-up timber suggests several things: lifeless wood that feels nothing, like someone who attends a gathering of revelation but is unmoved by what they hear; timber left leaning without serving a useful purpose, occupying space without contributing to learning, striving or calling people to Allah; and, in another interpretation, comfortable self-importance, sitting apart from ordinary believers.

Separate pieces of timber also lack a true bond, fitting people who each make their own interests paramount. Believers can use this description to examine themselves: do the calls of the Quran and Sunnah keep reaching me while I remain unresponsive and give nothing? The hypocrites’ inner instability also produces constant fear. They fear a revelation exposing their hearts, and every cry of war alarms them because they have no conviction on which to stand; they wait to see who wins so that they can join that side.

The warning against them thus concerns a concealed enemy within the ranks. An open enemy’s position is known, but a hidden one can influence the vulnerable, apparently adding to the group’s numbers while weakening it from within.

63:5.heading: Ayah 5

blocks.text: When it is said to them, “Come, so that the Messenger of Allah may seek forgiveness for you”, they shake their heads, and you see them turning away in arrogance.

When invited to let the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) seek forgiveness for them, they do not welcome the opening to forgiveness and return to Allah. They twist their heads and turn away arrogantly. At the beginning of the surah, their disguise consisted of emphatic testimony and oaths; when genuine submission and acknowledgment of wrongdoing are required, the arrogance beneath it emerges. This arose in the context of someone who denied what he had said and swore that he had said nothing.

Offered the opportunity to seek forgiveness, he remained obstinate, contradicting his earlier profession of faith. [The Arabic verb «يَصُدُّونَ» can express turning away themselves or turning others away as well; a translation may convey only one of these senses.] Hypocrisy often does more than reject the truth: it seeks an environment that justifies the rejection and draws others into it. Words of faith can be easy, but the moment of admitting fault, submitting and returning to Allah reveals the heart’s sincerity.

63:6.heading: Ayah 6

blocks.text: It is the same to them whether you seek forgiveness for them or not, Allah will never forgive them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wicked people.

The statement that seeking forgiveness for them makes no difference follows their persistence, arrogance and refusal to return to Allah. It does not mean that mercy is narrow or that seeking forgiveness has little value. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) deeply desired people’s guidance, yet the concern of someone calling others to Allah cannot produce guidance in a heart that clings to disobedience and refuses the repentance offered to it. This is why the verse ends by explaining that Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient. The danger is becoming so accustomed to departing from Allah’s commands that even the opportunity to return feels burdensome. When sin changes from a lapse for which one seeks forgiveness into a position one defends while arrogantly refusing repentance, the heart has entered a more serious condition.

63:7.heading: Ayah 7

blocks.text: They are those who say, “Do not spend on those who are with Allah’s Messenger so that they may desert him. But to Allah belong the treasures of the heavens and earth, but the hypocrites do not understand.

The verse exposes a central means of breaking the believers’ unity: using financial pressure to make people leave the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him). The aim is not merely to withhold money, but to disperse those gathered around him. In Zayd ibn Arqam’s account, he heard Abdullah ibn Ubayy make this statement and the statement in the following verse. Abdullah and his companions then denied it under oath, until Allah revealed the surah confirming Zayd’s account (Sahih al-Bukhari 4901).

This connects with the preceding surah, Al-Jumu‘ah: there, commerce and worldly attractions can draw people away; here, the hypocrites try to disperse them by withholding worldly support. The aim is the same: to break the gathering founded on faith. The Quran answers a purely material calculation with the truth that the treasures of the heavens and earth belong to Allah. Visible means exist, but provision ultimately rests with Him.

Understanding this requires insight beyond material appearances, which the hypocrites lack. Their question is how to scatter the believers; the faithful response is to ask how to unite them: removing rancor, supporting those in need, giving generously and preventing pressure from tearing them apart. Preserving unity requires effort and giving to counter the effort spent on destroying it.

63:8.heading: Ayah 8

blocks.text: They[2] say, “When we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the weaker therefrom.” In fact, all might belongs to Allah and to His Messenger, and to the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.

The threat to expel the supposedly weaker people from Madinah reveals the hypocrite’s measure of honor: tribe, wealth, influence and visible power. He portrays believers as needy and humiliated so that people will leave them. The verse corrects that measure at the level of faith: true honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger and the believers. Financial hardship or military defeat does not by itself erase the dignity of faith when faith remains firm in the heart.

The statement arose after a dispute during an expedition. When the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) heard what Abdullah ibn Ubayy had said, Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) asked permission to kill him. The Prophet replied: “Leave him, so that people will not say that Muhammad kills his Companions.” This shows wisdom in responding: not everything that can be done should be done immediately. The consequences of a decision and how people will understand it matter; opponents should not be handed material that drives people away from the religion.

This restraint allowed falsehood to expose itself until many who had been influenced by Abdullah ibn Ubayy turned away from him. Confronting a concealed enemy requires understanding his reality, exposing his contradictions and winning people over, rather than acting rashly in a way that enables greater harm.

63:9.heading: Ayah 9

blocks.text: O you who believe, do not let your wealth and your children distract you from Allah’s remembrance. For whoever does that, it is they who are the losers.

After describing the hypocrites, the surah addresses a matter that directly concerns the believer’s heart: wealth and children must not distract from remembering Allah. One interpretation addresses those who professed belief while concealing hypocrisy, but the warning here is understood as addressing believers so that they do not take the first steps along that path. Remembering Allah includes affirming His oneness, the Quran and the religion as a whole; the warning goes beyond neglecting remembrance with the tongue.

It concerns allowing personal advantage to take precedence over Allah’s command. Hypocrisy makes self-interest its governing principle: lying when lying serves it, betraying when betrayal serves it, and dissolving stable moral commitments in the face of desire. The danger begins before full hypocrisy, as love of this world grows and the connection with the Quran, gatherings of faith and nourishing acts of worship weakens.

A person can find themselves midway through a journey that demands patience and sacrifice, having lost the convictions that sustained them. The Prophetic warning about hardships on the path to Paradise and desires on the path to Hell also appears in another narration: “Hellfire is surrounded by lusts, and Paradise is surrounded by adversities.” A heart drawn toward this world and repelled by the Hereafter, or burdened by prayer, gatherings of faith and reminders, needs treatment rather than resignation to its condition.

Just as a fever prompts someone to investigate an illness, these signs call for self-examination before hypocritical traits accumulate. The loss described at the end of the verse is the loss of something once possessed, then neglected until it slipped away.

63:10.heading: Ayah 10

blocks.text: And spend from what We have provided for you before death comes to one of you, then he would say, “My Lord, If only You had delayed me for a short while, so that I would give in charity and be one of the righteous.”

The warning is followed by a practical remedy: spending from what Allah has provided before death arrives. Earlier, the hypocrites sought to withhold money in order to disperse the believers; at the end of the surah, believers are called to give. Giving itself becomes practical resistance to a mentality that uses wealth to divide and control. When death comes, the priorities concealed by desire become clear, and a person longs for a little more time to give charity and become righteous.

At the end, they recognize that what they needed was not to cling more tightly to worldly possessions, but to give and live uprightly. The request to return when death becomes apparent shows that the problem was not always ignorance of the truth: a person may know what should be done and still be held back by desire and procrastination. The Quran therefore makes the remedy known now: give from Allah’s provision before the wish to act remains but the time to act is gone.

63:11.heading: Ayah 11

blocks.text: But Allah will never delay a soul when its appointed time comes, and Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

The certainty that Allah will not delay a soul once its appointed time arrives cuts at the root of procrastination. Another opportunity is not guaranteed, and no one can postpone death until the circumstances they have been waiting for finally suit them. The verse can therefore serve as a practical reminder whenever a person hesitates to obey Allah or postpones a good deed. Hesitation and continually waiting to see what happens bring the heart closer to the mentality of hypocrisy; acting promptly preserves the truth it has recognized.

The closing statement that Allah is fully aware of what people do reaches beyond outward actions to the motives behind them: was the delay caused by a genuine excuse, or by attachment to this world, fear for personal interests and indecision? After a surah exposing hypocrisy concealed behind appearances and words, this ending is fitting. Allah knows the inward reality that people may not see; an appearance of faith cannot save a heart that puts off responding until its time runs out.
